sections.html:
Madison County is in east central Indiana, and its seat is Anderson. Population in 2020 was 130,129 for the county and 54,788 for Anderson. Besides Anderson, the county has the city of Alexandria and part of Elwood, plus smaller communities such as Ovid and Edgewood Village. The land is nearly flat, with some hills along the White River and Fall Creek.

The median home here is worth $147,700 and was built in 1965. That is an older housing stock, which is worth knowing whether you are arguing about an assessment or trying to sell a house that needs a new roof, furnace or plumbing.

sections.h2: Who handles Madison County property tax
sections.html:
Property tax runs through three offices in Anderson, and each one answers a different question. The Auditor and Treasurer both sit in the Government Center at 16 East 9th Street, Anderson, IN 46016. A wrong turn costs a trip downtown, so find your question in the table first.

OfficeWhat it handlesWhere to reach it
AssessorAssessed values and Form 130 appealsAnderson
AuditorDeductions, deed transfers, redemption after a tax saleGovernment Center; (765) 641-9422 or (765) 641-9505
TreasurerCollects payments, online payment, tax sale paymentsGovernment Center, 16 East 9th Street

Office hours and holiday closings sit on the county's contact page. Ask the Treasurer about a value and you will most likely be sent to the Assessor.

The Auditor handles the homestead deduction, the over 65 deduction, the blind or disabled deduction and the veteran deduction. You can file online, and the online form asks for your parcel number. Add an email address before you submit so the office can reach you.

Gather these before you sit down to file:

  • Your parcel number, found on the tax bill.
  • An Indiana driver's license.
  • Social Security numbers, last five digits only, for you and a spouse.
  • For the over 65 deduction, an income tax return or a Social Security 1099.

A deduction follows the filer, not the house. The next owner has to apply for a deduction of their own after closing, so a bill that was low for you can come in higher for them. Ask the Auditor what happens to a deduction on your parcel when the deed transfers.

The spring bill is due May 10 and the fall bill November 10, both paid to the county Treasurer. If either date lands on a weekend or holiday, you get the next business day. The county's tax system takes online payments, which is the quickest way to get a receipt.

Miss a due date and the Treasurer adds a 5 percent penalty, as long as you catch up inside 30 days and the parcel carries no older balance. Wait past that window, or have back taxes already, and the penalty doubles to 10 percent.

Fall far enough behind and the parcel heads to the tax sale. Three or more delinquent installments make it eligible, and SRI Services hosts the county's sale listings online. Once a parcel is certified for the sale, it cannot be paid online. The Treasurer takes those payments in person by cashier's check, money order or cash.

Buying a parcel back after a tax sale or commissioners' sale is the Auditor's job, not the Treasurer's. Look at the Auditor's tax sale list before you set a closing date to see how close your parcel is to certification.

If your value looks too high, put your case on paper. Form 130 is filed with the county assessing official and ends up in front of the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals. June 15 is the deadline, and the year it counts toward depends on the date the county mailed your notice.

The process runs in steps:

  1. An informal meeting with the assessing official.
  2. A hearing before the board within 180 days of filing, with notice at least 30 days ahead.
  3. An appeal to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131 if you disagree, or if the board does not decide within 180 days.

An appraisal is optional. Recent sales of comparable homes are the best evidence you can bring, and with a county median of $147,700, a sale price near that range is a reasonable reference point if you think your value is too high.

Nobody is penalized for paying on last year's assessed value while an appeal is open. Lose the appeal and the difference comes due, so set that money aside.

sections.h2: What to settle with the county before closing
sections.html:
A handful of phone calls keeps a closing on schedule. Call the Treasurer first and learn which installments are paid. Next, ask the Auditor whether your deductions stop at the sale and whether the parcel is on the tax sale list. If an appeal is pending, tell the Assessor you plan to sell, because the result shapes the bill the buyer inherits.

Quote the parcel number on every call, since it keeps all three offices on the same record. An inherited house also needs papers showing who has authority to sign, and the title company will want them before it books a closing.

Come closing, the title company splits the year's tax between buyer and seller and pays any open balance out of your proceeds. Ask for its figures a few days early and compare them with the Treasurer's, so a mismatch gets fixed before you sign.

Madison County owners who sell as-is usually point to the age of the house and the repairs it needs: roof, plumbing and furnace costs, inherited homes, tenant problems and repair bills that exceed what the house would bring after fixing. If back taxes are part of the picture, a cash sale lets the title company pay the delinquent amount from the proceeds at closing.

Two waterways matter for flood questions: the White River through northern Anderson and Fall Creek in the south of the county. A house close to either should have its flood zone checked on the survey or the lender's determination.

Pull together your latest tax bill, proof of payment and any appeal paperwork before an offer arrives. Cash buyers skip the lender's appraisal and repair demands, which is where older houses often stall. Title and taxes still have to be settled.

A cash sale also skips the showings, the staging and the weeks spent waiting for a buyer's loan to clear. You pick the closing date with the title company, and you can sell with the repairs undone. The offer reflects the work the house needs, so expect a lower number than a fully fixed house would bring, and weigh that against the months of carrying costs you avoid.

To weigh your options, request a written cash offer and put it next to what a listing would leave you after repairs, showings and holding costs.

faqs.q: When is Madison County property tax due?
faqs.a: Spring and fall installments are due May 10 and November 10. A weekend or holiday pushes the date to the next business day, and payment goes to the Treasurer.

faqs.q: Where is the Madison County Treasurer?
faqs.a: In the Government Center at 16 East 9th Street, Anderson, IN 46016. The county's contact page lists hours and closings.

faqs.q: Can I pay Madison County taxes online?
faqs.a: Yes, the Treasurer takes online payments. A parcel certified for tax sale cannot be paid online and needs a cashier's check, money order or cash in person.

faqs.q: Who handles homestead deductions in Madison County?
faqs.a: The Auditor's Office. Bring the parcel number, an Indiana driver's license and, for most filers, partial Social Security numbers for you and a spouse.

faqs.q: What makes a Madison County property eligible for the tax sale?
faqs.a: Three or more delinquent installments. Listings run online through SRI Services, and buying the parcel back goes through the Auditor.
